analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $250 a month per person in employer and marketplace plans.
analysis.headline: The bill capped monthly drug cost-sharing at $250 per person and $500 per family, but it never received a vote and died in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a hard limit into federal law: no one in an Affordable Care Act marketplace plan or an employer health plan could be charged more than $250 a month per person, or $500 per family, in out-of-pocket costs for covered prescription drugs. The limit would rise each year with medical inflation. It was introduced in December 2021, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and sent to its Health Subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2023 without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in marketplace or employer health plans who take expensive drugs and currently face out-of-pocket charges that can run into thousands of dollars a year. The cap applies per person and per family, with yearly inflation adjustments.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Affordable Care Act so that, starting in 2023, cost-sharing for covered prescription drugs in a qualified health plan cannot exceed $250 per month per enrolled individual, or $500 per month per family.
The same limit is extended to group health plans, which cover most workers with job-based insurance, by tying employer plan rules to the Affordable Care Act cost-sharing limits.
After 2023, the $250/$500 amounts increase each year by the medical care component of the Consumer Price Index, so the cap does not erode with inflation.
The cap takes effect for plan years beginning after December 31, 2022.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, who absorb the difference when a patient's drug costs exceed the cap, and indirectly all plan enrollees, who could face higher premiums because the cap shifts costs from sick patients to the whole risk pool.

drawbacks.text: The cap limits what patients pay out of pocket but does not lower drug prices themselves; the money above the cap shifts to the insurer and ultimately to premiums spread across all enrollees.
It applies only to marketplace plans and employer group health plans; it does not cap drug cost-sharing in Medicare, where many seniors with high drug costs are covered.

Insurers facing an out-of-pocket cap could respond by covering fewer drugs, charging higher premiums, or steering patients to cheaper alternatives, an effect a well-designed version would need to guard against.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people on costly prescriptions, the cap delivers real, immediate relief — $250 a month is a hard ceiling instead of an open-ended bill. But it treats the symptom: patients pay less at the counter while the underlying drug prices are untouched, so the cost shows up in premiums that everyone with insurance pays, and Medicare beneficiaries get nothing. A stronger bill would have paired patient relief with price limits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Manning introduced the Capping Prescription Costs Act of 2021 in the House on December 9, 2021, joined by five original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Health.

The full text shows the bill would cap prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person and $500 per family per month in marketplace plans starting in 2023, with the same limit applied to employer group plans and annual inflation adjustments.
Nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The action history shows no markup, vote, or further committee action through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, who would have absorbed the difference between patients' capped out-of-pocket costs and the actual price of expensive drugs, are better off that the bill died. Drug manufacturers also keep the status quo, since the bill never pressured their prices. Patients with high drug costs are left exactly where they were, with no federal cap on monthly prescription cost-sharing.

for.name: Rep. Kathy Manning
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five original cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Frank Pallone (D)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on December 10, 2021 and never scheduled a markup or vote in the remaining thirteen months of the Congress

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No member cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no bipartisan base that could push it toward a vote

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: A hard $250-per-month cap on drug cost-sharing forces insurers to absorb the gap between what patients pay and what expensive drugs actually cost, likely raising premiums across the risk pool. The industry's interest in the bill's death runs directly against patients' interest in relief.

The bill never touches drug list prices, so makers keep their pricing power; lower patient out-of-pocket costs could even increase sales by improving adherence. They lose nothing from the bill's failure.
